notes.meaning: God commands Israel to observe a release every seven years. During this seventh year, also known as the sabbatical year, normal farming ceased and debts were relieved among the covenant people. It taught God's people to trust His provision rather than their own financial gain.

Every lender was forbidden from demanding payment from a fellow Israelite during this year of release. Because the Lord Himself proclaimed this time, the lender was to honor God by letting go of the debt. Commentators differ on whether this cancelled the debt permanently or merely paused demands for payment during that fallow year.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that while ancient rabbinic tradition saw this as a complete wiping out of the debt, modern Catholic commentators generally hold that it only suspended the obligation to pay during that fallow year.

notes.meaning: An Israelite creditor could still demand payment from a foreign traveler or merchant, but had to release what was owed by a fellow Israelite brother. Foreigners were not bound to rest from business in the sabbatical year, so they still had income to pay their debts. This rule protected poor covenant members without showing malice toward outsiders.

Moses explains that the goal of this law was to eliminate extreme poverty from the community. God promised to pour out such rich blessings in their inheritance that no one would need to suffer in want, as long as the people carefully obeyed all His commandments. Obedience would ensure plenty for all.

Because the Lord would bless Israel as He promised, the nation would be wealthy enough to lend to many foreign nations without needing to borrow. Their financial strength would make them influential leaders rather than subjects to other peoples. Being in a position to lend was a mercy meant to encourage generosity toward others.

If any fellow Israelite in any town fell into poverty, the people were commanded not to turn cold or close their hands. Instead, they were to open their hands wide and freely loan him enough to meet his actual need. True charity begins with an open, compassionate heart toward a needy neighbor.

God warns against a selfish, wicked thought that might arise as the seventh year approached. A person might refuse to lend because the year of release would soon cancel or pause the debt. If the poor man cried to the Lord in his distress, God would hear him and hold the lender guilty of sin.

Israelites were to give generously and with a willing, cheerful spirit rather than a grudging heart. God promised that when they gave freely, He would bless all their work and daily efforts. Giving to the poor does not ruin a person, because God repays it with His favor.

There will never cease to be poor people in the land who need help. For that reason, God directly commands His people to keep their hands open wide to their brothers and the needy. God leaves room for the poor among us to test and cultivate our love and compassion.

If a fellow Hebrew, man or woman, had to sell themselves into servitude because of debt or poverty, they were to serve for only six years. In the seventh year, the master was required to grant them their freedom. God did not allow His people to remain permanent slaves to one another.

When setting a Hebrew servant free, the master was forbidden from sending them away empty-handed. The master had to give them a generous supply from the flock, the threshing floor, and the winepress, sharing the blessings God had provided. This gave the freed servant the supplies needed to start a new life rather than falling right back into debt.

Israel was told to remember that they had once been mistreated slaves in Egypt until the Lord rescued them. Because God redeemed them and did not send them away empty, they were obligated to show the same mercy to their own servants. Remembering God's rescue inspires generous treatment of others.

If a servant loved the master and the household and preferred not to leave, he could choose to remain for life. The master was to take an awl and pierce the servant's ear into the doorpost as an outward sign of willing, permanent devotion, and the same principle applied to female servants. Freedom was a right, but a servant was never forced away from a safe and loving home.

Masters were not to feel resentful or consider it a hardship when freeing a servant. Six years of dedicated service had provided far more benefit than paying a regular hired laborer, who received regular wages for shorter terms. God promised to bless the master in everything he did for honoring this command.

All firstborn male cattle and sheep belonged to the Lord and had to be set apart for Him. The owners could not work a firstborn ox in the field or shear the wool from a firstborn sheep for their own profit. Giving the firstborn honored God as the rightful owner of all their herds and flocks.

Each year, the family was to take these firstborn animals to the central place of worship chosen by the Lord and eat them in a holy feast before Him. This shared meal reminded the entire household that their food and possessions were gifts from God's hand. Joyful worship was built into the daily life of every family.

If an animal had any serious blemish, such as being blind, lame, or deformed, it could not be offered as a sacrifice to the Lord. God demands the best rather than flawed leftovers, and unblemished sacrifices also pointed forward to Christ as the perfect Lamb without defect. What is offered to God must honor His holiness.

A blemished firstborn animal could still be eaten at home in their towns like common wild game, such as deer or gazelle. Because it was not a sacred sacrifice at the altar, anyone could eat it, whether they were ceremonially clean or unclean. God did not waste the meat, even though it was unfit for the sanctuary.

The people were strictly forbidden from eating the animal's blood, which had to be poured out on the ground like water. God repeated this command often to emphasize respect for life, which belongs to Him alone. God's people must honor His boundaries in all everyday activities, including how they prepare their meals.
